summary: This memo is a glossary of networking terms specific to the Internet, written to help people new to the field. It is informational and was replaced by RFC 1983.

plainLanguage.summary: A glossary is a small dictionary. This one explains the strange words people use when talking about the Internet. A newer edition replaced it.

questions: what do internet networking terms mean
subtitle: An alphabetical dictionary of Internet and networking terms for newcomers.

tldr.problem: Internet users and networking newcomers encounter many acronyms and technical terms with no accessible reference for beginners.
tldr.mechanism: This glossary provides short, plain-language definitions of Internet-specific terms, organized alphabetically and cross-referenced, covering protocols, concepts, organizations, acronyms, and even Internet culture (like smiley faces).
tldr.outcome: Newcomers can quickly look up what TCP, IP, FTP, DNS, ARPANET, and hundreds of other terms mean. RFC 1983 replaced it with an expanded version.

today: RFC 1983 superseded this glossary with an expanded and revised version.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
Many networking glossaries exist, but this one focuses on terms specific to the Internet. The glossary includes basic terms and acronyms that other entries reference. For example, you will find both "TCP/IP" and the fuller entries for Transmission Control Protocol and Internet Protocol.

The document is organized alphabetically, with cross-references throughout to help readers navigate between related terms. Some entries include a source notation (such as RFC 1208 or "FYI") that credits where the definition originated. The glossary was created by the User Glossary Working Group of the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF).
sections.plainLanguage: A glossary is a mini dictionary. This one explains Internet and networking words in the order of the alphabet, with references to other words that are related.

sections.title: Networking Concepts and Protocols
sections.content:
The glossary covers fundamental networking concepts such as bandwidth, datagram, packet switching, connection-oriented and connectionless communication. It explains protocols like TCP (Transmission Control Protocol), UDP (User Datagram Protocol), IP (Internet Protocol), DNS (Domain Name System), FTP (File Transfer Protocol), and Telnet. Many entries describe the layers of the network stack: application layer, transport layer, internet layer, and link layer.

Other concepts include authentication, encryption, firewalls and security terms (hacker, cracker, virus, worm), as well as network devices (router, gateway, bridge, modem). The glossary explains addressing (IP address, MAC address, port), network topologies (Ethernet, token ring), and network organizations (autonomous system, backbone).
sections.plainLanguage: The glossary explains the big ideas about how networks work: how data travels, how computers find each other, and what different devices do.

sections.title: Organizations, Standards, and Acronyms
sections.content:
The glossary includes entries for important organizations like DARPA (Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, which funded the Internet's development), NSF (National Science Foundation), IETF (Internet Engineering Task Force), CERT (Computer Emergency Response Team), and IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers). It explains standard-setting bodies like ANSI, ISO, CCITT, and references to their standards (such as 802.x for Ethernet standards).

Many acronyms appear throughout: ARPANET (the predecessor to the Internet), BSD (Berkeley Software Distribution), TCP/IP, HTTP, SMTP, SNMP, and dozens of others. Some entries define historical networks like Bitnet and CSNET, which connected academic institutions before they joined the Internet. The glossary even includes light-hearted entries like ":-)", the emoticon for a smile in the flat medium of text communication.
sections.plainLanguage: The glossary lists the big organizations that created the Internet, the abbreviations they use, and the standards they came up with. It even explains funny things like smiley faces that people type in messages.

sections.title: What the Glossary Covers
sections.content:
The glossary is not comprehensive for all of computer science or networking; it concentrates on Internet-specific terms and concepts. You will find entries for email, web concepts, and Internet-related standards, but not general computer programming or operating system terms (except where they relate to Internet usage, such as Berkeley Software Distribution). Some entries reference RFCs (Requests for Comments) where fuller specifications can be found.

The glossary covers terms used across different layers and contexts: a novice user learning to send email, a system administrator configuring a network gateway, and a researcher developing new protocols all need to understand different subsets of these terms. The glossary serves all these audiences by providing short, clear definitions.
sections.plainLanguage: The glossary focuses on Internet and network words, not programming or computer basics. If you need to understand how the Internet works, you will find most of what you need here.

sections.title: Context and Internet History
sections.content:
Many glossary entries include historical context. For example, ARPANET is described as a pioneering long-haul network funded by ARPA that served as the basis for early networking research and the development of the Internet. DARPA (the renamed ARPA) is credited with funding the development of TCP/IP, Berkeley UNIX, and many other foundational Internet technologies.

The glossary captures the state of the Internet in early 1993, when networked computing was rapidly evolving. It references technologies and organizations that were cutting-edge at the time (such as Kerberos for authentication, ATM for bandwidth allocation, and the emerging World Wide Web infrastructure). Some technologies mentioned, such as CSNET, are noted as no longer operational.
sections.plainLanguage: The glossary explains where the Internet came from and who built it. It shows what people were using in the early 1990s, which helps you understand how the Internet grew into what it is today.
